6
A ball is kicked so that it has an initial velocity of 12 m s–1 at an angle of 50 to horizontal ground.
Assume that air resistance is negligible.
12 m s–1
50
What is the maximum height above the ground that is reached by the ball?
A
0.47 m
B
3.0 m
C
4.3 m
D
7.3 m

hints: Notice the launch diagram shows $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $50^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, so only part of the velocity acts vertically.
Recall vertical motion controls the height: the vertical component is $12 \sin 50^{\circ}$ and vertical velocity becomes zero at maximum height.
Connect this to $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ vertically with $v = 0$ and $a = -g$, then solve for the upward displacement $h$.
walkthrough: Resolve the initial velocity into vertical and horizontal parts. Height depends only on the vertical part: $u_y = 12 \sin 50^{\circ}$.
At maximum height the vertical velocity is $v_y = 0$, with acceleration $a = -9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. Use $v_y^2 = u_y^2 + 2ah$.
Rearrange for height $h$: $0 = u_y^2 - 2gh$, so $h = u_y^2/(2g)$.
Substitute values with units: $h \approx (9.19)^2/(2 \times 9.81) \approx 84.5/19.62 \approx 4.3 \text{ m}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Too small by about a factor of 10 and inconsistent with a $9 \text{m s}^{-1}$ vertical launch speed rising against $9.81 \text{m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: This is the height obtained from the horizontal component $12 \cos 50^{\circ}$ instead of the vertical component.

C.explanation: Matches $u_y = 12 \sin 50^{\circ}$ used in $h = u_y^2/(2g)$, giving about $4.3 \text{ m}$.

D.explanation: This is the height obtained using the full $12 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ as if launched vertically, ignoring the $50^{\circ}$ projection.
